To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) the number of publications in the area of traditional and syndromic infectious disease surveillance is increasing rapidly, 2) the majority of publications are from the United States, 3) the majority of studies are descriptive in nature, and 4) the majority of published articles are not available online.

(1) traditional surveillance of infectious diseases is still the most important tool to detect outbreaks, (2) syndromic surveillance can be useful to detect outbreaks of infectious diseases, (3) syndromic indicators are useful in combination with traditional surveillance, and (4) the usefulness of syndromic surveillance is limited in countries with a high incidence of infectious diseases, because the number of false positives is high.

1) the use of syndromic surveillance in the absence of a clear definition of syndromes, or of the syndromes that are of interest, can lead to the detection of a large number of events that are not of public health interest and that are not related to infectious diseases.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of methods for monitoring infectious diseases and pathogens, with the ultimate goal of reducing morbidity, mortality and economic burden.
the application of mathematical modelling to infectious diseases.
the development of new methods and systems for the detection of infectious diseases and their pathogens.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the use of the Internet and other forms of communication technology in the field of infectious diseases and public health has been and continues to be a valuable and effective tool for surveillance.

traditional and syndromic disease surveillance are both effective and efficient in detecting and reporting infectious diseases and pathogens, however traditional disease surveillance has been proven to be more effective in the detection and reporting of infectious diseases and pathogen.
there are a number of factors that contribute to the success of a syndromic surveillance system, but the most important factor is the availability and quality of the underlying data.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have been working on a variety of topics in the area of surveillance of infectious diseases.
we have shown how the combination of traditional and syndromic disease surveillance systems can be used to improve the detection and investigation of infectious disease outbreaks.
we have developed new methods for detecting and characterising infectious diseases and pathogens, and we have demonstrated their value for public health.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the use of syndromic data is a promising tool for early detection of outbreaks of infectious disease.
the two methods of surveillance complement each other, and together provide a more robust and accurate picture of disease activity.
syndromic surveillance is not a replacement for traditional surveillance.
